6.129: So, we haven't had the problems in a lot of these elite units with recruiting the way I think your more regular military has. And to the extent that we do, I'll tell you why. Despite losing an eye and losing friends, deployments were the best, best time of my life.
6.130: You have to be a little bit of a sociopath to understand that. But guess what? You need those kind of warriors to defend you. And those are the people I want in the military. But to expand on your question, because I think what you might be getting at is, there's a lot of—because I get asked this question a lot by parents. They're like, "Should I send my kid to the military? Is it too woke?" That's where the politics comes in. And I'm like, "No. I mean, you should still send your kid to the military because it's still an awesome place."
6.131: And yes, there's always going to be some idiots that are doing some stupid things at their command that are the opposite of making it a lethal war-fighting capability. And that's especially true in the last few years. But it's few and far between. It's still a good place to be, and it's going to set you up for success. So, I still believe in our military. Lecture 7: Serving the People At a glance — Serving the people.
7.1: OK, so this is, this is part two of the same lecture, right? A day in the modern Congress. So today we're going to talk about the job of a congressman. And I'm going to describe our job in three categories.
7.2: One, you vote on legislation, OK, so that's the most obvious one. Your district elects you so that there's one vote cast for or against every single bill that comes to the floor. Second, your job is to communicate with constituents, with the public. And third, you're basically a customer service agent for the federal government.
7.3: So, casting votes on bills, I mean, that's like the, that's the most basic of functions. It's the most minimal of duties. And, and it's also one you really can't hide from. If you get elected— and in theory, you could do this—if you get elected, you could take a two- year vacation. You really could. The only reason anyone would even know about it is because your voting history would be blank.
7.4: And if you want to do more than just cast votes, and luckily most members do, then your job is to actually draft legislation. Now, of course, there's a good chance that you'd get fired by your voters if your voting record was a total blank slate. So nobody actually takes a two-year vacation. If you want to do more than just cast votes, and luckily most members actually do want to do more than that, well, then your job is to draft proposals for legislation. And then you got to muscle your way through the process that we went over yesterday.
7.5: OK, so implicit in that duty is meeting with constituents. You meet with stakeholders, you meet with interest groups, you meet with outside experts. You're doing your best to understand their niche issues. Now there's an endless supply of these meetings. Everybody wants to meet with you, so you got to manage them to the best of your ability.
7.6: But if you're in the minority party, the truth is, you aren't doing as much legislating as you would like. In the majority, well, you've got more of a shot at making a difference. But even then, your position matters quite a bit. So, if you've been around long enough and you're in a position of leadership, like a, like a ranking member or a chairman, just to be clear, a ranking member just means you're at the top of the committee, but you're in the minority. A chairman means you're in the majority, so you're the chairman; you're actually in charge.
7.7: So if you're in one of those positions, you might actually find yourself with some ability to negotiate a deal here or there. But most members are not in that position. So what do you do instead? You talk. Lots of talking. Politicians like to talk. You advocate publicly for the issues you care about, and then you also criticize the decisions of the other side, hoping that, come election season, voters are more persuaded to give your party more power to implement some of the issues that you've been beating the drum about.
7.8: So you see a whole slew of tools to do that, from speeches on the House floor to news interviews to social media. Each office is also allowed a budget for what's called franking. Franking is an official communication with your constituents. It's either via regular mail or email. Now, there's actually strict rules around franking. You can talk about policy, you can talk about legislation. You usually are talking about what kind of legislation that you have passed and that you are championing. You're telling your constituents what you're doing.
7.9: OK, there's nothing wrong with that. That's your job. But what you can absolutely not do is talk about your election. You can't advocate for your own reelection. You cannot talk about the opponents in your election. Now you can also use your office budget to sponsor events, events like a town hall or other policy-related events. So we talked about town halls and meet-and-greets and all that, but we can do policy events, too, and those are really cool.
7.10: So, for instance, every year I do what's called a health care innovation summit. This is one of my favorite things I do, and I bring in entrepreneurs in the health care space and interview them on stage, kind of like a TED Talk, but an interview. And I'm interviewing them about, like, a new therapy or a new device, a new treatment. And it's open to the public. Anybody can come. And it's nonpartisan. It's a fun, nonpartisan, educational way that we can inform and engage with our constituents.
7.11: The last part of our job, and probably the least talked about, is our job as a customer service agent for the federal government. So back in your district office, meaning for me, back in the Houston area, you'll hire a few people called caseworkers. They take calls daily from constituents and they hear about their problems with the federal government. It's not a complaint line, OK? It's not. At least it's not supposed to be. We put those calls to the interns.
7.12: They are the ones who take the notes about how I've sold out my country or I'm a crooked career politician or whatever else the caller comes up with. No, the caseworkers are dealing with real problems. They're dealing with a veteran trying to fix their benefits at the VA. They're dealing with a flood victim trying to get an answer from FEMA. Or they're dealing with a poor planner who didn't realize their passport expired and they need one expedited for their upcoming trip to Cancun.
7.13: That actually happens a lot. But you have no idea how many constituents are super thankful that our office got them their passport when they needed it. So you know what? Public service. Now, most members engage in all of these duties with fervor. Some don't. Again, in theory, you don't have to do any of this stuff. You don't have to do any travel. You don't have to do any of those CODELs. You don't have to even hire anybody.
7.14: You could take a two-year vacation. I mean, really, you could. You have no boss to report to, except the voters. They're your boss. Now if you take that two-year vacation, you're probably going to lose your election because your bosses, the people, well, they're going to fire you.
7.15: There is one other way to get fired. And you can get fired if two-thirds of the members of the House vote to expel you. This happened pretty recently, with George Santos. This practice has usually been reserved for pretty extreme cases of wrongdoing, but George Santos had some pretty extreme cases. But in theory, you could expel a member for any reason at all. I mean, maybe they smell bad. Maybe they refuse to use the right parking spots. That annoys a lot of people.
7.16: The Congress is not a court of law. It's under no obligation to act with the same robust evidentiary standards as a court. Expelling members or even impeaching a President is largely a political act and with only vague guidelines outlined in the Constitution. Now this was actually by design. The courts have their place, with due process and requirements for compelling evidence to be presented in a formal court setting.
7.17: But the procedures in Congress are designed around the principle of checks and balances, which is why you might see what you might consider frivolous reasons for impeachment that would not necessarily hold up in the court of law. Is that OK? That the right thing to do? I don't know. You tell me.
7.18: So there was a lot of debate about presidential impeachment in the years leading up to the ratification of the Constitution. Should this be a strictly judicial process to be decided by the Supreme Court? I mean, maybe, at first glance, but doesn't the President appoint those judges? Can they be impartial? Would the Senate be a better body for that kind of judgment, even accounting for the obvious and potential politicization?
7.19: So they wrestled with these questions, and we still do today. I mean, they wrestled with what constitutes high crimes and misdemeanors exactly. There's not actually a good definition for these terms. So scholars have forever debated their meaning. I mean, many have said high crimes is not necessarily referring to, like, a really bad law being violated, but an action that is bad for the nation, which is an inherently subjective thing to say.
7.20: But it has to be bad enough to get the House to vote on articles of impeachment, and for two-thirds of the Senate to find the accused guilty. So these actions are indeed political. That's OK. Politics is the manifestation of public opinion, which is an important part of democracy. So the impeachment process, in my view, is a political process, and it's essential to our notion of checks and balances.
7.21: So, Hamilton seemed to agree. So I think I'm in good company here. So in Federalist 65, Hamilton wrote, "A well-constituted court for the trial of impeachments is an object not more to be desired than difficult to be obtained in a government wholly elective." You really just do have to appreciate how they write back then.
7.22: "The subjects of its jurisdiction are those offenses which proceed from the misconduct of public men or, in other words, from the abuse or violation of some public trust. They are of a nature which may with peculiar propriety be denominated political, as they relate chiefly to injuries done immediately to the society itself."
7.23: OK, so he's acknowledging that impeachments can be political. Now he then wrestles with the question of who best to arbitrate said impeachment. He says, "The prosecution of them, for this reason, will seldom fail to agitate the passions of the whole community, and it divide it into parties more or less friendly or inimical to the accused. In many cases, it will connect itself with pre-existing factions.
7.24: "It will enlist all of their animosities, partialities, influence, and interest on one side or the other; and in such cases, there will always be the greatest danger that the decision will be regulated more by the comparative strength of parties, than by the real demonstrations of innocence or guilt."
7.25: He's kind of, like, counterarguing against himself here. He knew that politics would play a role, and he also knew there just wasn't an easy way around that, except to ensure that the process would be very, very difficult. And so I would point out the following. It's not exactly easy to succeed in making what one might believe is a frivolous or a political impeachment. And so while it's, it's certainly possible, it remains extremely rare and extremely unlikely.
7.26: President Trump was impeached twice, never convicted by the Senate. The House recently voted to impeach Secretary of Homeland Security Alejandro Mayorkas. Senate never even glanced at it. So both sides will argue that each of these impeachment cases was political. Now my response to that is, OK, yeah, so what?
7.27: That's what checks and balances means. It means the ability to rebalance in the rare instance of overwhelming public support. And it has to be pretty overwhelming for the Senate to convict with a two-thirds majority. And you might also consider this. When it comes to real crimes, we already have an entire third branch of government. It's called the judicial branch.
7.28: That's where the courts are. That's where you provide evidence. That's where you convict people. That's why the impeachment process is indeed political and allowed to be political and actually preferred to be political. It has to come from the people. It's the people's last resort. That's what it is. OK, so let's talk now, as I promised, about the types of members. This is where things get interesting.
7.29: There's a lot of types of members of Congress. There's many different ideas is of what the purpose of a congressman is. And there's also plenty of political science literature on the subject as well, but I'll just give you my take. Now, the most commonly taught categories of representation are these two, trustees and delegates.
7.30: A trustee is entrusted with the decision-making power on behalf of their constituents. It's understood that the constituency can't collectively make decisions about every niche subject in Congress, and so they entrust their representative to do that for them.
7.31: Now the whole point of the election process is for voters to get a feel for what kind of decisions that representative might actually make. They might ask questions like, well, "How do they approach problems? What experiences inform their stances? How are they qualified? Are they long-term thinkers, short-term thinkers? Are they just telling me what I want to hear? Are they just going to go along with the party line or are they going to occasionally veer from that?" You'll pick up on those kind of things during an election, or at least you hope you will.
7.32: Now, the delegate, just a mouthpiece. A delegate isn't really supposed to make decisions based on their best judgment, but instead upon the wishes of the people that they represent. Now you might imagine a delegate taking a poll on every single vote that we take in Congress, and then voting accordingly.
7.33: Now, of course there's some pretty obvious problems with that. First of all, I don't know how hundreds of thousands of voters can stop what they're doing every day, study a bill, and then cast their vote in a poll. Like, I don't care how good technology gets. That's just, this is not plausible. This is not a feasible option.
7.34: Furthermore, a system like that would be massively influenced by interest groups, knowing that they can affect public opinion with targeted ads, with messaging. Now that happens already, of course, but it would happen times a thousand if you had this make-believe environment where you literally took polls from your district before every single vote.
7.35: So, I consider myself a trustee representative. I told people who I was when I ran for Congress, and I continue to tell them every single day. I make my opinions known. I explain what my governing philosophy is, and you can take it or leave it. Now, it's hard to find anyone that you actually agree with 100% of the time. But if you find yourself disagreeing with me over 50% of the time, you might want to vote for somebody else. That's OK. That's democracy.
7.36: But every member is a bit of a mix of a trustee and delegate. That's the truth. There are some issues that I vote upon strictly because of the interests of my district. But at the same time, you know, most of those interests, they actually line up pretty well with my own personal philosophy. So I don't really have any contradictions to speak of.
7.37: There's other times where I just don't have that strong of opinion on a matter. That's rare, but it does happen. And so you might, you know, might go back to your district and just kind of see what people are thinking. On contentious votes, now there's a number of factors that I might consider, and this goes for all congressmen. This is sort of how, this is how we analyze votes. So I'm going to give you an example.
7.38: Let's take the example of the debt ceiling increase of 2023. Now this is always a contentious vote for Republicans, especially Republicans, because you know, we're the party of fiscal responsibility. We can't vote to increase the debt ceiling. So the base of the party and the political entertainment industry that riles them up are by, by default, they're always against a debt ceiling increase, every single time. If you poll them, they won't give it a second thought. They'll just say, "No. Vote no. We're against it."
7.39: I'm not talking about every Republican. I'm just talking about the hyper-passionate base that's made up of activists, radio talk show hosts, social media influencers, you know, anyone who generally imbibes partisan news all day long. They're going to say no. I know that. They're always going to say no to that. They're going to say no to budgets. They're going to say no to a lot.
7.40: So, here's what I do. I start to ask my staff, OK, how many calls are we getting about this? Who is calling in? And are they from the district? That's another thing that matters. Or are they just outside groups that have, that have acted, because this happens a lot. Groups will activate a lot of members throughout the country, and they'll say, "Call the, call your representative's number." And then we just get flooded with calls, but they're not even from our district.
7.41: And then I ask them to assess online media activity. Like, who's writing about this? Who's talking about this? Let's see how much the public is really caring about it. And then we'll maybe call local community leaders. Who's talking about it back home? Let's get their assessment. Now, in this particular case, when it regards the debt ceiling, I'm not doing all of that analysis to help, to help inform me how I should vote, yes or no.
7.42: This is the debt ceiling, so I already know what the right choice is. I have to vote yes. Because if I vote no and it actually, and it actually fails, we get economic collapse. That's actually what happens if you don't raise the debt ceiling. So I'm doing this political analysis in this case to gauge whether or not I'm going to be facing a political firestorm when I get home, and I need to prepare for that.
7.43: On other votes, where I just personally don't have a strong conviction, it's possible, I may indeed do that same analysis. But to gauge how I actually vote, again that's kind of rare. But many members are indeed of the delegate mindset. And so they default to no, not because they think they should default on our debt. Right. They're hitting no, but they're hoping it passes. They know better. They're not that stupid. Some are. Most aren't. They know better.
7.44: They know the economy would crash. They know that defaulting on our debt actually costs us more money because interest rates skyrocket. They know all of this, and yet they still vote no. This is the delegate mindset. They look at what the political entertainment industry is saying and they follow along with the script.
7.45: Members like this, and there's too many of them, I don't think they take responsibility for their vote. That's my opinion. They see their vote, like, as a virtue signal to the public. I don't. I think it should be a definitive yes or no decision that you're making. It's irresponsible to just see it as a virtue signal. I try to see my vote as a deciding vote. I try to pretend like my vote is the one vote. I try to pretend like it all rests on my shoulders.
7.46: This mindset forces you to do the hard work of weighing the pros and cons of each vote, because you don't get to press a button called perfect. There's yes and there's no. The yes one is green, the red one is no. It's really, really obvious. There's a third button. It's called present. But, like, no one gets any respect for voting present. I mean, it's like ordering non-alcoholic beer at a party. I mean, don't trust that guy.
7.47: As you're probably aware, there's quite a few members from each side of the aisle that self-label as anti-establishment hardliners, purists, whatever. They always vote against the big important stuff. Military funding? Nope. Debt ceiling increase? No. Continuing resolution to keep the government funded and stop it from shutting down? No. Renew farmers' crop insurance, keep American agriculture afloat? Nope.
7.48: Here's the thing about legislating and being in Congress, and especially in a Congress where, let's be honest, there's a diffusion of responsibility, right? Because there's so many of us, 435. You can find a problem with every single bill that you vote on. It's the easiest thing in the world to do. Now when they can't find anything in it that they don't like, they'll find things that aren't in it, and then complain about that.
7.49: Because the military funding bill, you know what, didn't cure cancer, can't vote for it. You know, I joke that these forever-no voters, they should just save the taxpayers some money and just fire their entire staff. Honestly, they don't need them. They're not doing the work of objectively assessing the good and the bad of every bill and making a hard decision.
7.50: A lot of them talk like they do. They talk like they're experts on every subject and like they're the only patriots who noticed the hidden dangers of each piece of legislation. Most of the time, I'll be honest with you, most of the time their arguments are twisted or just outright wrong. I'm just speaking from experience. I could give you examples, but if you follow my history on social media, you've probably seen me take on those battles a few times.
7.51: So, now's not the time to name names. So we've talked about trustees, we've talked about delegates. That's your typical political science lesson, but that barely scratches the surface of the modern Congress. And I'm going to give you some more categories, Dan's categories, based on my experiences.
